A spangle is a small, thin, flat, shiny disc or piece of glittering material. Its defining quality is that it catches light and throws it back brilliantly, creating a sparkling, eye-catching effect. Think of the tiny, circular, glittery decorations you see sewn all over a dancer's costume or a glamorous party dress — those are spangles.

A spangle is very small — typically no bigger than a fingernail, often much smaller. It is flat, not three-dimensional. It is made of metal, or a metallic material, so its surface is shiny and reflective. When light hits a spangle at any angle, it bounces off and glitters. When hundreds of spangles are sewn closely together on a piece of fabric, the whole surface seems to shimmer and sparkle as the wearer moves.

Spangles appear most commonly on clothing and costumes that are meant to dazzle — circus performer outfits, ballroom dancing costumes, stage and theatre costumes, cheerleading uniforms, and glamorous evening gowns. The purpose is always decoration and visual brilliance: a garment covered in spangles is impossible to ignore under a spotlight.

You may already know the word "sequin." A sequin and a spangle refer to essentially the same object — a small, shiny, flat disc used as a decorative ornament on clothing. "Sequin" is the more modern and widely used term, while "spangle" is older and somewhat more literary or formal in feel, but they describe the same thing. If you can picture a sequined dress, you can picture a spangled one.

Beyond the literal physical object, "spangle" is also used figuratively to describe any small, bright, sparkling point of light — something that glitters the way a real spangle does. In this sense, stars in the night sky are often called spangles in poetry and descriptive writing, because they appear as tiny, brilliant points of light scattered across a dark background, just like glittery discs scattered across dark fabric.

This figurative sense is exactly where the phrase "Star-Spangled Banner" — the title of the American national anthem and a name for the American flag — comes from. The flag is "star-spangled," meaning it is covered with stars that glitter like spangles. The stars on the flag act as the spangles; the flag is the fabric they are scattered across.

"Her costume was covered from top to bottom in silver spangles, and she blazed like a mirror ball under the stage lights."

"Looking up at the clear night sky, he saw thousands of spangles scattered across the darkness."

"The old ballroom gown had lost several of its golden spangles, leaving small bare patches on the bodice."
The single idea to hold onto

Whether used literally or figuratively, a spangle always means the same fundamental thing: something small, flat, shiny, and brilliantly glittering — a tiny concentrated point of sparkle. The word carries a sense of glamour, decoration, and light. Wherever there is deliberate, decorative shimmer — on a costume, in the sky, on a surface — the word "spangle" fits perfectly.
